doc.title: Chris Parker interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, January 5, 2023

title: Playing as a leader versus as a sideman
summary: As leader of his trio he plays his own tunes exuberantly; as a sideman he is a supportive accompanist; he mentions East Coast Meeting.

story.theme_name: Leading a band: choosing, paying and managing players
story.community_name: Leading a band: running, choosing and keeping players

blocks.x: You have led your own groups and I wonder if you play differently when you are leading a group than when you are not?

Oh yeah. My trio is, I’m there to — a lot of them are my compositions, most of them are. So I want to play them as exuberantly as I can because I’m still exploring the tune and what feels good and what’s going to work in a certain section and what’s going to sound good behind the soloist and if I’m a sideman, if I’m backing somebody up I’m much more respectful of their vocal or the horn player, what they’re doing. I want to be supportive. I want to be a good accompanist not a solo artist and not a drummer/composer. So yeah, there’s a big difference between the two. And it depends on the type of group that I’m leading too. You know if it’s my trio it’s one thing and if it’s an R & B kind of thing, like a new group I have called East Coast Meeting with a singer and a keyboard player. There are individual compositions but I want my voice to be integral to the group itself. So yeah.
